1. Vide the present commercial suit, plaintiffs seek permanent injunction restraining infringement of trademark, dilution, passing off, unfair competition, damages, rendition of accounts etc. against defendant.

2. Briefly stated, facts of the present case as averred in the plaint are that plaintiff no.1 is the proprietor of M/s EXPOSE APPARELS as well as one of the Directors of plaintiff no.2 which is a Private Limited Company incorporated under The Companies Act.

Plaintiffs are engaged in the well-known and well-established business of manufacturing and marketing inter-alia of Readymade Garments, Wearing apparels, Hosiery, Under Garments, Fashion wears and Fashion accessories (hereinafter referred to as the "said goods").
3. Plaintiff No.1 is the owner and registered proprietor of trademark "X'POSE" by virtue of application dated 08.03.1994 under No.621615 in class 25 in respect of the "said goods".
The said trademark was coined and adopted by plaintiff no.1 in the year 1993 and since then has been used continuously, extensively and exclusively.
The plaintiff no.2 is using the said trademark "X'POSE" of the plaintiff no.1 by way of permitted use.

4. It is also the case of the plaintiffs that the plaintiff no.1 also represents its trademark "X'POSE" in an original, Digitally signed by HEMANI CS (COMM.) plaintiffs have earned goodwill and reputation, so much so that the trademark "X'POSE" is exclusively identified with the plaintiffs.

6. Plaintiff has also incurred huge expenses to promote his product under the trademark "X'POSE"
through various medium of advertisements.

Similarly, the sales grew from 8.91 lacs in 1995-96 to Rs.2593 lacs in 2021-2022.

19. Now, examining the ratios of the judgment cited by learned counsels for the parties in the context of Section 29(1) and (4) of the Act.

Section 29 (1) & (4) (a) of The Act postulates that :
(1) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who, not being a registered proprietor or a person using by way of permitted use, uses in the course of trade, a mark which is identical with, or deceptively similar to, the trade mark in relation to goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered.

sentences.text: "When a person gets his trade mark registered, he acquires valuable rights by reason of such registration.

Registration of his trade mark gives him the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in connection with the goods in respect of which it is registered and if there is any invasion of this right by any other person using a mark which is the same or deceptively similar to his trade mark, he can protect his trade mark by an action for infringement in which he can obtain injunction, damages or an account of profits made by the other person.
In such an action, the registration of a trade mark is prima facie evidence of its validity. "

Thus, reinforcing the principle that registered owner of a trademark, need not prove its use to seek injunction from the person invading his right.
21.
Learned counsel for plaintiffs to further hammer this principle of law, also relied upon judgment titled as DALIP CHAND AGGARWAL AND ORS (SUPRA).

In this case, respondent company was manufacturing and selling various agricultural equipment, razor blades, tractors, washing machines,
motorcycles, shock absorbers, thermometers and other medical appliances since 1951.
In 1951, the respondent also obtained registration of its trademark of the word "Escorts" relating to electric irons, electric kettles, shouldering irons and elements for electric irons and kettles.

In 1953, the appellant sought registration of trademark 'Escort' in respect of electric irons, electric kettles,
shouldering irons and elements for electric irons and kettles.
The respondents filed an opposition to the CS (COMM.) NO.561/2023

In appeal, the Hon'ble Single Judge of Delhi High Court allowed the opposition on the ground that registration of the trademark 'Escort' in favour of the appellant is likely to deceive the public.

In the appeal against the judgment of Hon'ble Single Judge, the Hon'ble DB upheld the order of the Hon'ble Single Judge opining that:
It cannot be forgotten that the word 'Escorts' was in the market right from 1951 onwards with a very considerable sale.

It is correct that prior to 1961 the goods which were sold by respondents were different but that will not take the case out of Section 11 and would atleast show some indication as to why the appellant had used the word 'Escort'.

Considering however, that the respondents were in field with the trade mark even though of other goods from 1951 onwards and considering that there was a very small amount of goods sold by the appellant in a period of a year or two prior to the registration by the respondents, the onus which was on the applicant, was rightly held not to have been destroyed.
We, therefore, see no infirmity in the Judgment of the learned single Judge.
The appeal is, therefore, dismissed.

The defendant contended that his company had acquired a reputation around the world by the name of Honda.

33. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi applied the test of Goodwill in this matter and held that the act of the defendant "caused damage to the reputation of the plaintiff as the defendant's trademark "HONDA" for a pressure cooker is deceptively similar to that of the plaintiff's".
Also, it creates puzzlement in the psyche of the purchasers.

Hence, the court restrained the defendant from using the mark "HONDA" in respect of pressure cookers or any other allied and cognate goods or any other trademark which were identical with and deceptively similar to the trademark HONDA and to do anything which amounts to passing off their goods as the goods of the plaintiff.
34. In this judgment, the Hon'ble High Court also reiterated the settled law w.r.t. passing off action.

It held as under:-
"14.

In a nutshell, in an action for passing off, the plaintiff has to establish that his business or goods has acquired the reputation he is claiming, by showing that, his trade name has become distinctive of his goods and the purchasing public at large associates the plaintiff's name with them.
The plaintiff is, however, not required to establish fraudulent intention on the part of the defendant.
Causing of actual confusion amongst the customers is also not to be proved.
What is required to be established is the likelihood of deception or CS (COMM.) NO.561/2023

The plaintiff, however, need not prove actual loss or damage in an action of passing off.

43. As observed above, the concept of passing off is a tort and with the passage of time, with the developing case law it has changed and now the two traders need not necessarily operate in the same field so as to suffer injury on account of the goods of one trader being passed off as those of the other.
44. With the changed concept of passing off action, it is now not material for a passing off action that the plaintiff and the defendant should trade in the same field.
I find that some business are truly international in character and the reputation and goodwill attached to them cannot in fact be held being international also.
The plaintiff's business is of international character and obviously the reputation and goodwill attached to its trade mark HONDA is also of international repute.

The plaintiff's trade mark HONDA, which is of global repute, is used by the defendants for a product like pressure cooker, to acquire the benefit of its goodwill and reputation so as to create deception for the public who are likely to buy defendant's product believing the same as coming from the house of HONDA or associated with the plaintiff in some manner.

By doing so, it would dilute the goodwill and reputation of the plaintiff and the wrong committed by the defendants would certainly be an actionable wrong and the plaintiff is within its rights to ask for restraint against the defendants from using its mark HONDA for their products."
